body:
• The Justice Department sued Arkansas, Hawaii, Utah and Washington, D.C. on Sept. 10, bringing its campaign against in-state tuition for noncitizens to 25 lawsuits nationwide.
  • The Arkansas suit targets a 2019 law — signed by Republican Gov. Asa Hutchinson and passed with bipartisan support — letting immigrants who lived in the state three years and graduated from an Arkansas high school pay in-state tuition, including DACA recipients, work-permit holders and Marshall Islands immigrants.
  • The DOJ calls the laws "blatant unequal treatment" of U.S. citizens and unconstitutional under federal law, citing a 1996 statute; it says six prior suits have already produced favorable court orders.
  • Arkansas' Republican attorney general agrees with the DOJ that the state law should not be enforced, while immigrant advocates call the suits an unprecedented attack on tuition-equity laws.

The final four

The Justice Department said Thursday it has now sued every state with laws granting in-state tuition to noncitizens, filing its final four complaints against Arkansas, Hawaii, Utah and Washington, D.C. The lawsuits — announced in press release No. 26-1039 dated Sept. 10, 2026 — bring the administration's total to 25 challenges against so-called Dream Act tuition policies.

The complaints ask federal judges to block enforcement of state laws requiring colleges to charge in-state rates to noncitizens who maintain in-state residency, regardless of lawful presence, and to bar financial assistance and scholarships for them. "This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens," said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the DOJ's Civil Division. "This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country."

"No more placing illegal aliens over American citizens on this Department of Justice's watch. We have now sued every state across our Nation that has a state law or regulation granting illegal aliens in-state tuition."

— Stanley E. Woodward Jr., Associate Attorney General

The Arkansas law at issue

The Arkansas suit challenges a 2019 law signed by then-Gov. Asa Hutchinson, a Republican, that allows immigrants who have lived in the state for at least three years and graduated from an Arkansas public or private high school to pay in-state tuition at state colleges and universities. The law covers DACA recipients, people with work permits or whose parents hold them, and immigrants from the Marshall Islands. As originally drafted it applied to immigrants regardless of legal status, but it was narrowed to the three categories before passing with bipartisan support in the majority-Republican Legislature.

Hutchinson signed the tuition measure alongside a bill letting the state issue nursing licenses to DACA recipients. "We're a welcoming state, and we want to be able to continue that," he said at the time.

The DOJ's complaint calls the law unconstitutional "blatant unequal treatment," arguing it violates a 1996 federal statute that bars states from offering postsecondary benefits to unlawfully present residents unless U.S. citizens receive the same benefit regardless of their state of residence.

A campaign with wins — and backlash

The department says the strategy is working: six lawsuits in Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska, Illinois and Kansas have produced orders permanently enjoining similar laws, including a Fifth Circuit ruling. A federal judge in Kansas struck down that state's 2004 tuition law just a day before the new filings. Suits remain pending in 15 more states, including California, New York, Virginia and Arizona.

In Arkansas, the state's Republican Attorney General Tim Griffin is siding with Washington. "We agree with the U.S. Department of Justice that federal law preempts state law in this case, and that this state law should not be enforced," spokesperson Jeff LeMaster said.

The push traces to an April 2025 executive order directing the attorney general to identify and stop enforcing state policies favoring noncitizens. "This coordinated attack on the rights of young immigrants is unprecedented and unwarranted," said Thomas A. Saenz, president and general counsel of MALDEF.

"It's disingenuous to say it's a law for 'illegal aliens,' and it's a political stunt."

— Megan Godfrey, former Arkansas state Representative

Godfrey, a Democrat who co-sponsored the 2019 law, said the suit mischaracterizes it. The law's supporters argue it keeps high-skilled students — raised and educated in Arkansas — in the state, benefiting its economy.

What is next

Federal judges will now decide whether the 2019 Arkansas law — and the tuition-equity policies in Hawaii, Utah and D.C. — survive. With six states already enjoined and 15 cases pending, the administration's 25-suit sweep is moving toward a definitive national answer on whether states can extend tuition benefits to noncitizens. For students relying on in-state rates this academic year, the outcome could change the cost of a college degree overnight.
diaspora_angle: The outcome matters well beyond Arkansas: immigrant families across the 25 sued states — including Indian students and work-authorized families paying in-state rates — face the prospect of sharply higher college costs.
headline: Justice Department Sues Arkansas Over In-State Tuition for Immigrant Students
subheadline: Thursday's lawsuits against Arkansas, Hawaii, Utah and D.C. bring the administration's total to 25, as the DOJ says it has now challenged every state offering tuition breaks to noncitizens.
